item.title: Installation
item.description:
This page covers how to install the Joulie simulator in a Kubernetes cluster.

Prerequisites

  • A running Kubernetes cluster (real or kind for local development)
  • kubectl configured for the target cluster
  • helm v3+ (for Helm installation)

Install via Helm (recommended)

The simulator is published as an OCI Helm chart. Install it with:

helm install joulie-sim oci://registry.cern.ch/joulie/joulie-sim \
 -n joulie-system --create-namespace

To customize values, download the default values first:

helm show values oci://registry.cern.ch/joulie/joulie-sim > values.yaml

Then install with overrides:

item.title: Workload and Power Simulator
item.description:
The Joulie simulator lets you run full control-loop experiments on virtual clusters without real hardware. It keeps Kubernetes scheduling real while simulating hardware telemetry, power dynamics, and thermal behavior per node.

This page covers the simulator’s architecture, HTTP API, and integration points. Detailed subsystems are documented on dedicated pages linked throughout.

Architecture at a glance

The simulator extends the same control path used on real nodes:

  1. Node labels define simulated hardware identity.
  2. The controller manager resolves hardware from NodeHardware when available, otherwise from labels/inventory fallback.
  3. The controller manager writes desired node profile (NodeTwin.spec).
  4. Agent reads desired state and sends control intents.
  5. Simulator emulates telemetry/control behavior per node and exposes HTTP endpoints.
  6. Next reconcile loop reacts to updated simulated state.

The diagram shows the end-to-end loop:

item.title: Simulated Cluster
item.description: The simulated cluster runs the real Joulie components on emulated bare-metal nodes, on one machine with Docker. The agent discovers and caps emulated hardware through the same files and tools it uses on a real node, the controller manager reads node power from the simulator’s OpenTelemetry metrics in Prometheus, and the scheduler extender scores real pods. The scripts in scripts/simcluster drive it, tests/simcluster checks it end to end, and CI runs it on every pull request that touches what it builds.

item.title: Workload Scenarios
item.description: A workload scenario runs a workload through the simulated cluster and checks what happened: whether the jobs completed, where they were placed, how long they took, what energy they used, and how Joulie’s settings compare with each other or with no Joulie at all. The jobs are real Kubernetes Jobs, scheduled by the real scheduler and the Joulie extender onto KWOK Nodes, and the simulator’s v1 workload engine drives them on the emulated hardware, so a cap the agent writes slows the jobs on that Node.

item.title: Workload Generation
item.description:
This page documents how Joulie generates realistic AI workload traces for the simulator.

It is separate from Workload Simulator:

  • this page explains how traces are generated,
  • the workload-simulator page explains how those traces are consumed at runtime.

Scope

The current generator is designed to be realistic for:

  • AI-oriented Kubernetes clusters,
  • CPU + GPU workloads,
  • memory-pressure-sensitive jobs,
  • multi-pod logical workloads such as distributed training and HPO-style experiments.

item.title: Workload Distributions
item.description:
This page documents the statistical distributions and priors behind the current workload generator.

Use it together with:

  • Workload Generation
  • Workload Simulator

What this page is for

The generator is no longer just a flat random-job emitter. It now uses explicit priors for:

  • arrival timing,
  • GPU-count skew,
  • duration shape,
  • utilization,
  • memory pressure,
  • multi-pod workload structure.

item.title: Kubernetes AI Workloads
item.description:
This page explains how the logical workload structures used by Joulie map onto common Kubernetes-native AI workload patterns.

It is mainly a documentation page today. The current simulator generator emits the structure metadata and pod-expanded jobs, but it does not yet render PyTorchJob, MPIJob, or Katib Experiment manifests directly.

Why this page exists

The workload-generation report makes an important point:

  • realistic AI workloads are often not single pods,
  • and a single logical workload may map to:
    • a launcher + workers,
    • parameter servers + workers,
    • or a controller + many HPO trial pods.

That distinction matters even in a simulator, because power and slowdown should often be understood at the logical workload level, not only at the pod level.

item.title: Workload Simulator
item.description:
This page documents the workload-side simulation model.

Trace generation methodology, statistical priors, multi-pod workload structure, and workload-generation references are documented in Workload Generation.

Scope

The workload simulator handles:

  • trace/job ingestion,
  • pod creation and placement via real scheduler,
  • per-job progress updates,
  • completion and pod deletion,
  • class inference from scheduling constraints.

Power/control dynamics are documented separately in:

  • Power Simulator

Trace-driven workload model

Enable with:

  • SIM_WORKLOAD_TRACE_PATH=/path/to/trace.jsonl

The simulator loads type=job records and schedules pods over time according to submit offsets.

item.title: Power Simulator
item.description:
This page describes the simulator runtime mechanics (control/state/energy paths).

The canonical physical model, provenance, and hardware assumptions are documented in:

  • Hardware Modeling

For workload progression semantics:

  • Workload Simulator

Scope

The power simulator runtime is responsible for:

  • keeping per-node control state (CPU cap, DVFS throttle, GPU cap),
  • applying control actions from /control/{node},
  • updating dynamics with settling/ramp behavior,
  • exposing power telemetry on /otlp/telemetry/{node} and /telemetry/{node} (OTLP JSON; /telemetry/{node}?format=legacy serves the deprecated legacy JSON until v0.4.0),
  • integrating energy over time (/debug/energy).

item.title: Hardware Modeling
item.description:
This simulator section now treats hardware modeling as a shared hardware concept rather than a simulator-only detail.

The canonical page is:

  • Hardware Modeling and Physical Power Model

Use that page for:

  • CPU and GPU model provenance
  • physical assumptions behind caps and slowdown
  • heterogeneous-node semantics
  • current limitations and calibration status

From the simulator point of view, the important relationship is simple:

  • the simulator implements the modeling assumptions documented there
  • the agent relies on the same hardware assumptions when interpreting caps and backend limits
  • simulator runtime pages describe how those models are exercised in experiments

item.title: Hardware Calibration
item.description:
hwcalib fit (simulator/cmd/hwcalib, package simulator/pkg/calib) fits the physics of a hardware profile to a sweep measured on one of your nodes, and writes the result as a local profile the simulator loads from SIM_PROFILES_DIR. The builtin profiles keep vendor figures and placeholders; a calibrated profile replaces them with what your machine draws. hwcalib sweep records such a sweep on the node itself (see Recording on the node).

Recording a sweep

A sweep holds the node at a series of setpoints and records, at every sample, the node’s readings and the setpoints it held. Each setpoint should last long enough to settle: the fit drops the start of every setpoint (see Segments and steady windows) and needs at least 5 samples after that, so with a 2 s sample period a setpoint of 22 s or more is enough.

item.title: Simulator Metrics
item.description:
The simulator publishes three kinds of telemetry:

  • Prometheus metrics about itself at /metrics (joulie_sim_*), for Prometheus to scrape.
  • OpenTelemetry metrics and events about the emulated nodes and the facility, in emulate mode only. Metrics are pushed as OTLP JSON over HTTP; events are written to events.jsonl and pushed when a logs endpoint is set.
  • Compatibility exporters, in emulate mode only: the Prometheus formats of real exporters (Kepler, dcgm-exporter) at /exporters/<name>/metrics, opt-in.

The OpenTelemetry names are spelled once, in pkg/otel/semconv, and the controller manager reads the same names back from Prometheus. Their Prometheus spelling is computed by pkg/otel/promname. A contract test (tests/contracts/otel_docs_test.go) fails when this page misses a name of that table, names one the table does not define, or gives a name another unit, instrument, attribute list, severity or Prometheus spelling than the table.

item.title: Model Changes
item.description:
This page lists every change since Joulie v0.2.3 that moves the numbers the simulator produces for its modelled nodes (standalone mode, and Kubernetes mode without emulation), and how far each one moved them. A result produced with an older simulator holds for the model it ran; read it together with this table. Emulated nodes (SIM_EMULATE) run the physics of simulator/pkg/hwemu and are not covered here.

The reports of experiments 01 to 03 in experiments/ were produced before every change below and have not been rerun; each carries a dated note that says which of its model statements did not hold.
